title: CTRL-FM: Inference-Time Structural Control for Flow-Based Virtual Sensing under Long-Horizon Node Outages

paper.title: CTRL-FM: Inference-Time Structural Control for Flow-Based Virtual Sensing under Long-Horizon Node Outages
paper.abstract: Abstract Long-horizon node outages are harder than conventional missing-value imputation because complete sensor trajectories remain unobserved for extended periods, while the usefulness of spatial and temporal dependencies varies across outage locations and operating regimes. Existing graph, diffusion, and flow-based methods typically impose a fixed structural bias, which can oversmooth abrupt changes or propagate errors from unreliable neighbors. We introduce CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time decision. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns a conditional velocity field while keeping observed measurements exactly fixed. For each realized outage, CTRL-FM constructs self-supervised proxy outages from surviving measurements and uses their known values to select among uncontrolled, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and balanced control policies. The selected policy is locally modulated by graph and temporal reliability estimated exclusively from surviving observations, while boundary-anchored trends provide structural guidance. Control is applied only to missing entries and is rejected when proxy evidence does not sufficiently improve over uncontrolled sampling. Across PeMS08, METR-LA, Air-36, and AQI, CTRL-FM achieves the strongest overall performance under 30% and 60% node outages. Stress tests with up to 75% sensor loss further show graceful degradation and consistent gains over training-time and fixed structural control. These results demonstrate that validating, selecting, and locally adapting structural guidance for each realized outage is more effective than imposing a single global structural prior.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Spatio-temporal graph imputation, also known as graph kriging or virtual sensing, reconstructs signals at unavailable locations from measurements observed across time and a sensor network. It supports applications in traffic monitoring, environmental sensing, climate analysis, and urban infrastructure management Yang et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Ye et al. (2021) ; Shen et al. (2023) . Given a multivariate graph signal, the goal is to recover missing node trajectories by exploiting temporal dynamics and dependencies among connected locations. Most existing methods focus on randomly missing entries, short gaps, or moderate sparsity. Real sensing systems also experience long-horizon node outages, in which complete sensors remain unavailable over extended contiguous intervals because of hardware failure, maintenance, communication loss, or sparse deployment Zhong et al. (2023) ; Jia et al. (2025) ; He et al. (2025) . This setting is substantially harder: failed nodes provide no direct evidence during the outage, temporal anchors may be distant, and multiple trajectories may be compatible with the surviving observations. Graph neural networks, diffusion models, and flow-based methods reduce this ambiguity by imposing graph connectivity, temporal continuity, or signal smoothness Wu et al. (2021a) ; Cini et al. (2022) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . However, the reliability of these assumptions depends on the realized outage and operating regime. Neighboring traffic sensors may enter different congestion states, environmental signals may change abruptly, and graph relations may become misleading during incidents, drift, or operational interventions Cuza et al. (2022) ; Xu et al. (2024) ; Khalili et al. (2026) . Consequently, a structural prior that improves one outage may oversmooth another or propagate errors from unrepresentative neighbors. Existing approaches typically encode structural guidance as a global modeling choice: it is embedded in the architecture, learned through training-time regularization, or imposed through a fixed sampling objective. Such strategies identify what is useful on average over historical masks, but they do not determine whether the same graph–temporal assumption is appropriate for the specific outage encountered at inference. Because the failed values are unknown, the model also lacks a direct mechanism for validating or rejecting its structural choice. We address this limitation with CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time control decision. CTRL-FM separates general reconstruction learning from outage-specific structural control. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns a reusable conditional velocity field while keeping observed measurements fixed throughout training and sampling. The backbone is then frozen, and its sampling velocity is adapted for each realized outage rather than retraining the model or applying a post-processing correction. At inference, CTRL-FM temporarily hides nearby surviving measurements to construct local self-supervised proxy outages. Because their values remain available as evaluation targets, these proxies allow the method to compare uncontrolled, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and balanced control policies under the current outage context. The selected policy is applied to the true outage only when it sufficiently improves over uncontrolled sampling; otherwise, CTRL-FM abstains from structural intervention. CTRL-FM further separates which policy should control an outage from where that policy should be trusted. Reliability modules estimate graph and temporal support exclusively from surviving observations, using local coverage, neighborhood agreement, change magnitude, graph distance, and proximity to observed temporal boundaries. Boundary-anchored guidance then connects the evolving flow velocity to valid observed trends, while missing-region projection and repeated clamping preserve every observed measurement exactly. We evaluate CTRL-FM on the PeMS08 and METR-LA traffic networks and the Air-36 and AQI air-quality networks under 30% and 60% long-horizon node outages, with additional stress tests up to 75% sensor loss. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we evaluate whether proxy outages provide a reliable self-supervised basis for policy selection through proxy coverage, agreement with retrospective oracle rankings, and oracle-policy match. Our contributions are: • We formulate structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time control problem and use local self-supervised proxy outages to select how the frozen flow velocity should be modified for each realized failure. • We combine observed-only reliability, boundary-anchored guidance, and conservative abstention to determine where structural correction is supported and when it should be rejected. • We develop an observation-preserving, missing-only flow-matching formulation that confines transport and structural control to unavailable entries while keeping all surviving measurements exactly fixed. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The Method section presents CTRL-FM, while the Experiments section evaluates reconstruction accuracy, efficiency, proxy validity, and robustness under severe outages.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.text: Classical spatio-temporal imputation methods rely on low-rank, tensor, statistical, or kernel assumptions Zhou et al. (2015) ; Lei et al. (2022) ; Wu et al. (2021b) . Neural approaches learn richer dependencies directly from data. BRITS Cao et al. (2018) and SAITS Du et al. (2023) primarily model temporal and cross-variable relationships, whereas IGNNK Wu et al. (2021a) , KCN Appleby et al. (2020) , GRIN Cini et al. (2022) , SPIN Marisca et al. (2022) , and OPCR Deng et al. (2024) exploit graph structure for spatial reconstruction. Inductive and graph-learning methods additionally support inference at partially or entirely unavailable locations Wu et al. (2021a) ; Appleby et al. (2020) ; Zhong et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . However, these methods generally apply a single learned reconstruction strategy across all outage configurations. Probabilistic methods address the ambiguity of missing trajectories by modeling conditional distributions. CSDI Tashiro et al. (2021) introduces score-based diffusion for time-series imputation, while PriSTI Liu et al. (2023) , CDSTE Lei et al. (2024) , Diffputer Zhang et al. (2025a) , and SSD-TS Gao et al. (2025) incorporate temporal, spatial, or geographic structure into diffusion-based reconstruction. Their structural conditioning, however, is typically fixed during training and reused for every test outage. Flow matching provides a continuous-time alternative to iterative diffusion sampling Lipman et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) . GiFlow Zhang et al. (2026) applies graph-informed flow matching to spatio-temporal imputation, while training-free guidance methods modify frozen flow models through auxiliary sampling objectives Wang et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2025) . These methods commonly use a predefined structural objective or guidance strength, which may be unreliable when graph and temporal dependencies vary across outages. CTRL-FM instead treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time decision. It uses self-supervised proxy outages to select among graph, temporal, balanced, and uncontrolled policies, modulates the selected policy using reliability estimated only from surviving observations, and abstains when structural control is not supported. Thus, CTRL-FM validates both when and where structural guidance should be applied for each realized outage.

sections.heading: 3.1 Outage-Conditioned Controlled Flow Matching
sections.text: Conventional conditional flow matching Lipman et al. (2023) learns a velocity field whose behavior is fixed after training. Although the field may condition on observations, masks, and graph structure, the same learned structural bias is reused across outages with different failed nodes and operating regimes. This is restrictive for long-horizon failures: graph neighbors may be informative for one outage but misleading for another, while strong temporal continuity may suppress peaks, drops, or regime transitions. CTRL-FM separates general reconstruction learning from outage-specific structural control. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns an observation-preserving transport field. At inference, local self-supervised proxy outages determine how the frozen field should be controlled, while observed-only reliability determines where the selected graph and temporal guidance should be trusted. The resulting correction is injected directly into the sampling velocity rather than applied after reconstruction. Figure 1: Overview of CTRL-FM. A missing-only flow backbone is trained while preserving observations. At inference, local proxy outages select an outage-specific policy, observed-only reliability modulates structural guidance, and the controlled velocity reconstructs only missing entries while maintaining exact observation consistency.

sections.heading: Datasets and outage protocol.
sections.text: We evaluate CTRL-FM on two traffic datasets, PeMS08 Chen et al. (2001) ; Guo et al. (2019) and METR-LA Li et al. (2018) , and two air-quality datasets, Air-36 Yi et al. (2016) and AQI Zheng et al. (2015) . Long-horizon outages are simulated by removing the complete trajectories of randomly selected nodes at outage ratios of 30% and 60%. For multivariate PeMS08, the same node mask is applied to flow, occupancy, and speed. All methods use identical chronological splits, outage masks, test windows, and failed-region evaluation sets. Dataset statistics, preprocessing, graph construction, and the complete outage protocol are provided in Appendix Section 2.1.

sections.heading: Baselines and controlled variants.
sections.text: We compare CTRL-FM with a non-learning Graph Neighbor baseline; deterministic neural imputers SAITS Du et al. (2023) , IGNNK Wu et al. (2021a) , GRIN Cini et al. (2022) , and OPCR Deng et al. (2024) ; probabilistic models CSDI Tashiro et al. (2021) , PriSTI Liu et al. (2023) , and CDSTE Lei et al. (2024) ; and the graph-informed flow-matching method GiFlow Zhang et al. (2026) . CDSTE is designed and evaluated only for traffic datasets. FM-TrainStruct uses the same backbone as CTRL-FM but incorporates structural regularization only during training. Fixed-CTRL applies one validation-selected control policy to all test outages, whereas CTRL-FM selects and modulates the policy separately for each realized outage. Detailed baseline descriptions are provided in Appendix Section 2.4.

sections.heading: Implementation and evaluation.
sections.text: Hyperparameters are selected on the validation split without access to test-outage values, and results are averaged over three independent runs. MAE measures pointwise error, CRPS Gneiting and Raftery (2007) evaluates probabilistic quality, and Peak- Δ \Delta MAE evaluates large temporal changes. MAE and Peak- Δ \Delta MAE are reported in original physical units after inverse normalization, whereas CRPS is computed in standardized space. All metrics are evaluated only on the true failed-node region; lower values are better. Training, calibration, and metric details are provided in Appendix Sections 2.2, 2.3, and 2.5.

sections.heading: 4.2 Validity of Proxy-Based Policy Selection
sections.text: This experiment tests whether nearby observed measurements can reliably guide policy selection. Valid-proxy coverage shows how often enough proxy data are available. Spearman’s ρ \rho measures whether proxy scores rank policies similarly to their true missing-region errors. Oracle match shows how often CTRL-FM selects the same best policy as a post-hoc oracle, which determines the best policy after reconstruction by comparing all policies against the true missing values. The post-hoc oracle is used only for retrospective diagnosis after all policy-selection, abstention, and reconstruction decisions have been completed. It is never used for proxy construction, policy scoring, hyperparameter selection, or final reconstruction. Table 1: Validity of proxy-based policy selection at 60% node outage. Valid proxy measures calibration coverage, Spearman’s ρ \rho measures agreement with the post-hoc true policy ranking, and oracle match reports selection of the true best policy. Higher values are better. Dataset Valid proxy (%) ↑ \uparrow 𝝆 ↑ \boldsymbol{\rho}\uparrow Oracle match (%) ↑ \uparrow PeMS08 98.7 0.82 88.4 METR-LA 99.1 0.79 84.8 Air-36 87.4 0.68 78.6 AQI 98.9 0.76 81.6 As shown in Table 1 , valid proxies are available for 98.7–99.1% of outages on PeMS08, METR-LA, and AQI. Coverage decreases to 87.4% on Air-36 because its network provides fewer surviving proxy candidates. Proxy rankings achieve correlations of 0.68–0.82 with the post-hoc oracle, and CTRL-FM selects the true best candidate in 78.6–88.4% of valid cases. These results support the use of local surviving measurements for policy selection without revealing failed-node values. Formal definitions are provided in Appendix Section 2.5, and selected-policy frequencies are reported in Appendix Section 2.8.

sections.heading: Main results.
sections.text: Table 2 reports the mean performance over three random seeds. CTRL-FM delivers the strongest overall results across all datasets and outage levels. On PeMS08, it achieves the lowest MAE, CRPS, and Peak- Δ \Delta MAE at both 30% and 60% outage. On METR-LA, it obtains the best MAE and Peak- Δ \Delta MAE under both settings, while CDSTE retains the lowest CRPS. For Air-36 and AQI at 30% outage, OPCR and GiFlow achieve the lowest MAE, respectively, whereas CTRL-FM provides the best CRPS and Peak- Δ \Delta MAE. Under the more severe 60% outage, CTRL-FM ranks first across all reported metrics on both air-quality datasets. These results show that outage-conditioned structural control is particularly effective as the available sensor support decreases. Complete results, additional baselines, and mean ± \pm standard deviation values are reported in Appendix Section 2.6; the main table reports means only.

sections.heading: Extreme-outage robustness.
sections.text: CTRL-FM remains the strongest of the evaluated controlled flow-matching variants on PeMS08, METR-LA, and AQI under 65% and 75% node outages. At 75% outage, valid-proxy coverage remains between 84.8% and 89.3%, despite the limited surviving support. These results demonstrate graceful degradation under severe sensor loss. sections.heading: Qualitative reconstruction.
sections.text: Figure 2 shows that CTRL-FM most consistently follows the ground-truth trajectories across flow, occupancy, and speed. sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Although CTRL-FM achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated methods and degrades more gracefully under severe outages, it still relies on sufficient surviving observations to construct informative proxies and on a sensor graph that captures meaningful dependencies. Performance may decline under extremely sparse or highly clustered failures. Future work should consider real outage events, larger networks, and adaptive graph structures.

sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework for long-horizon node outages that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time control problem rather than a fixed modeling assumption. Unlike approaches that impose the same graph and temporal constraints across different failure scenarios, CTRL-FM selects and adapts structural guidance based on the available observations and the characteristics of each realized outage. By separating reconstruction learning from inference-time structural control, the framework enables a frozen flow-matching backbone to adapt its sampling dynamics without retraining or modifying learned parameters. Specifically, self-supervised local proxy outages provide an evidence-based mechanism for evaluating candidate control policies, while observed-only reliability estimation and boundary-anchored guidance determine where graph and temporal information can be trusted. Conservative abstention further prevents structural intervention when proxy evidence does not sufficiently support improvement over uncontrolled sampling. Throughout this process, structural corrections remain restricted to missing entries, ensuring exact preservation of observed measurements. Experiments on four traffic and air-quality datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CTRL-FM under 30% and 60% long-horizon node outages, achieving the strongest overall reconstruction performance, particularly under severe sensor loss. Proxy-selection analysis demonstrates that surviving observations provide informative signals for identifying suitable control policies, while ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of reliability modulation and conservative abstention. Additional stress tests with up to 75% node outages show graceful performance degradation, with only modest computational overhead relative to the uncontrolled flow-matching backbone. Nevertheless, the framework relies on sufficiently informative surviving observations and meaningful spatial relationships, which may limit its effectiveness under extremely sparse or spatially clustered failures. Future work could explore adaptive proxy construction, dynamically evolving graph structures, and validation on real-world sensor outage events. More broadly, these findings suggest that structural guidance in generative reconstruction models can be validated and adapted at inference time rather than imposed uniformly across all scenarios, offering a promising direction toward more reliable and robust virtual sensing systems.

sections.heading: Chronological splits and normalization.
sections.text: Each dataset is divided chronologically into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test data. Temporal ordering is preserved to avoid future-information leakage. All variables are standardized using statistics computed only from the training split and transformed back to their original physical units before evaluation. PeMS08 flow, occupancy, and speed are normalized independently.

sections.heading: Graph construction.
sections.text: PeMS08 sensors are connected using the physical road topology, with edge weights derived from inter-sensor road distance. METR-LA uses its standard road-distance graph with thresholded Gaussian affinities. For Air-36 and AQI, monitoring stations are connected using geographic proximity, and pairwise distances are converted into thresholded Gaussian affinities. Edge weights are normalized, and the same graph is provided to all graph-based methods whenever their architectures support an external adjacency matrix.

sections.text: For every test window and outage ratio, we generate ten independently sampled failed-node sets. The number of evaluation outages is N out = N win ​ N mask , N mask = 10 . N_{\mathrm{out}}=N_{\mathrm{win}}N_{\mathrm{mask}},\qquad N_{\mathrm{mask}}=10. Each combination of one test window and one failed-node set is treated as one evaluation outage.

sections.heading: Paired evaluation and reproducibility.
sections.text: Training masks are sampled dynamically by varying the failed-node set across training windows. Validation and test masks are generated once, stored, and reused across all methods and experimental seeds. All methods therefore use identical test windows, failed-node sets, outage durations, and failed-region evaluation entries. For comparisons among FM-Base, FM-TrainStruct, Fixed-CTRL, and CTRL-FM, the initial Gaussian samples, sample budget, and numerical-solver grid are also shared whenever applicable. Model initialization, training stochasticity, and generative sampling vary across the three seeds, while the underlying evaluation outages remain fixed. Validation masks are generated independently from test masks and are used only for checkpoint selection, hyperparameter selection, candidate-policy selection, and selection of the globally fixed policy used by Fixed-CTRL. No value from a true test outage is used for training, validation, proxy construction, policy scoring, or reliability estimation.

sections.heading: True and proxy outage durations.
sections.text: The true outage spans the complete 24-hour traffic window or seven-day air-quality window. In contrast, CTRL-FM uses proxy intervals of L probe = 12 L_{\mathrm{probe}}=12 steps only for policy calibration, corresponding to one hour for PeMS08 and METR-LA and 12 hours for Air-36 and AQI. Proxy entries are temporarily hidden only from surviving nodes and never overlap the true failed-node region.

sections.heading: Evaluation region.
sections.text: All metrics are computed only on entries removed by the true test outage. Surviving measurements remain available as conditioning information and are kept exactly fixed throughout sampling. Temporarily hidden proxy entries are excluded from the model input, boundary guidance, and reliability features and are accessed only after reconstruction to evaluate candidate policies.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: The flow-matching backbone is trained with AdamW using a hidden dimension of 128, four graph-attention groups, batch size 32, and an initial learning rate of 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Training runs for at most 200 epochs with cosine learning-rate decay, a five-epoch warm-up, early-stopping patience of 20 epochs, weight decay of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , dropout of 0.1 0.1 , and gradient clipping at 1.0 1.0 . Training outages are sampled dynamically from the training split. The graph and temporal reliability modules are trained on synthetic training outages and frozen together with the backbone before test-time calibration.

sections.heading: Observation-preserving sampling.
sections.text: For each reconstruction sample, missing entries are initialized with standard Gaussian noise, while observed entries are fixed at their measured values. The resulting flow ODE is integrated using Heun’s method with S = 20 S=20 solver steps. The state is re-clamped after every solver stage so that only missing entries are updated. We generate S p = 20 S_{p}=20 samples per outage; their mean is used for point prediction, while the complete sample set is used to compute CRPS and predictive intervals.

sections.heading: Candidate-policy library.
sections.text: CTRL-FM uses the five predefined policies in Table 4 : uncontrolled, weak balanced, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and strong balanced control. The policy parameters ( α r , λ g , r , λ t , r ) (\alpha_{r},\lambda_{g,r},\lambda_{t,r}) are selected using validation outages and fixed before test evaluation. They are not optimized or updated at test time. Instead, CTRL-FM selects one of these fixed policies separately for each realized outage using self-supervised proxy calibration.

sections.heading: Proxy calibration.
sections.text: For each test outage, CTRL-FM constructs up to B = 4 B=4 proxy outages by temporarily hiding surviving nodes within r p = 2 r_{p}=2 graph hops of the true failed-node set. Each proxy covers L probe = 12 L_{\mathrm{probe}}=12 steps, corresponding to one hour for PeMS08 and METR-LA and 12 hours for Air-36 and AQI. For Air-36, which contains only 36 stations, the search begins within three graph hops and expands to all surviving stations when insufficient eligible proxy nodes are available. All five policies are evaluated on each proxy using the same Gaussian initialization and a reduced five-step Heun solver. The proxy score combines pointwise reconstruction error and temporal-change error with λ dyn = 0.5 \lambda_{\mathrm{dyn}}=0.5 . Proxy scores are weighted by their distance from the true failed-node set using temperature τ p = 0.5 \tau_{p}=0.5 , so nearby proxies contribute more strongly.

sections.heading: 2.4 Baselines and Controlled Variants
sections.text: We compare CTRL-FM against classical references, deterministic neural imputers, probabilistic generative models, and controlled variants built from the same flow-matching backbone. All methods use identical chronological splits, test windows, outage masks, and missing-region evaluation sets. A common graph is provided whenever the baseline supports an external adjacency matrix.

sections.heading: Classical references.
sections.text: Historical Average replaces each missing entry with the training-set mean for the same sensor, variable, and time-of-week position. When unavailable, it uses the corresponding sensor-variable training mean. Graph Neighbor reconstructs a failed sensor using a normalized weighted average of its surviving graph neighbors. The weights are renormalized over available neighbors, with Historical Average used when no neighbor remains observed. On PeMS08, the procedure is applied separately to flow, occupancy, and speed.

sections.heading: Deterministic neural baselines.
sections.text: SAITS Du et al. [2023] uses diagonally masked self-attention to model temporal dependencies and cross-variable correlations without an explicit sensor graph. IGNNK Wu et al. [2021a] learns inductive graph message passing through random-subgraph reconstruction and is designed for kriging at unobserved sensor locations. GRIN Cini et al. [2022] combines bidirectional recurrent modeling with graph message passing to propagate information across both time and connected sensors. OPCR Deng et al. [2024] performs separate one-step spatial and temporal propagation, followed by confidence-aware refinement of the initial estimates.

sections.heading: Probabilistic generative baselines.
sections.text: CSDI Tashiro et al. [2021] is a conditional score-based diffusion model that reconstructs missing values while conditioning on the observed sequence, without explicitly using a predefined sensor graph. PriSTI Liu et al. [2023] is a spatio-temporal diffusion model that constructs a global context prior from available measurements and uses temporal, spatial, and geographic dependencies during reconstruction. CDSTE Lei et al. [2024] combines conditional diffusion with a spatio-temporal estimator for traffic-state reconstruction at sensor-free locations. Because it is designed specifically for traffic data, it is evaluated only on PeMS08 and METR-LA. GiFlow Zhang et al. [2026] is a graph-informed flow-matching method whose source distribution is constructed through adaptive spatio-temporal filtering of observed graph signals. It is the closest external flow-based baseline to CTRL-FM.

sections.heading: Flow-matching backbone and controlled variants.
sections.text: FM-Base is the observation-preserving, missing-only flow-matching backbone without structural control. FM-TrainStruct adds graph and temporal regularization during training, producing a fixed structural bias at inference. Fixed-CTRL instead injects one validation-selected control policy into the frozen FM-Base sampling velocity for all test outages. CTRL-FM selects the control policy separately for each outage using self-supervised proxies, modulates graph and temporal guidance with observed-only reliability, and falls back to uncontrolled when proxy evidence is insufficient. All variants use the same backbone capacity, data splits, outage masks, sampling budget, and solver settings whenever applicable, isolating the effects of training-time, fixed inference-time, and outage-conditioned inference-time structural control.

Existing graph, diffusion, and flow-based methods typically impose a fixed structural bias, which can oversmooth abrupt changes or propagate errors from unreliable neighbors. We introduce CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time decision. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns a conditional velocity field while keeping observed measurements exactly fixed. For each realized outage, CTRL-FM constructs self-supervised proxy outages from surviving measurements and uses their known values to select among uncontrolled, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and balanced control policies. The selected policy is locally modulated by graph and temporal reliability estimated exclusively from surviving observations, while boundary-anchored trends provide structural guidance. Control is applied only to missing entries and is rejected when proxy evidence does not sufficiently improve over uncontrolled sampling. Across PeMS08, METR-LA, Air-36, and AQI, CTRL-FM achieves the strongest overall performance under 30% and 60% node outages. Stress tests with up to 75% sensor loss further show graceful degradation and consistent gains over training-time and fixed structural control. These results demonstrate that validating, selecting, and locally adapting structural guidance for each realized outage is more effective than imposing a single global structural prior. A Preprint 1 Introduction Spatio-temporal graph imputation, also known as graph kriging or virtual sensing, reconstructs signals at unavailable locations from measurements observed across time and a sensor network. It supports applications in traffic monitoring, environmental sensing, climate analysis, and urban infrastructure management Yang et al. (2025) ; Chen et al. (2025) ; Ye et al. (2021) ; Shen et al. (2023) . Given a multivariate graph signal, the goal is to recover missing node trajectories by exploiting temporal dynamics and dependencies among connected locations. Most existing methods focus on randomly missing entries, short gaps, or moderate sparsity. Real sensing systems also experience long-horizon node outages, in which complete sensors remain unavailable over extended contiguous intervals because of hardware failure, maintenance, communication loss, or sparse deployment Zhong et al. (2023) ; Jia et al. (2025) ; He et al. (2025) . This setting is substantially harder: failed nodes provide no direct evidence during the outage, temporal anchors may be distant, and multiple trajectories may be compatible with the surviving observations. Graph neural networks, diffusion models, and flow-based methods reduce this ambiguity by imposing graph connectivity, temporal continuity, or signal smoothness Wu et al. (2021a) ; Cini et al. (2022) ; Zhang et al. (2025a) ; Zhang et al. (2026) . However, the reliability of these assumptions depends on the realized outage and operating regime. Neighboring traffic sensors may enter different congestion states, environmental signals may change abruptly, and graph relations may become misleading during incidents, drift, or operational interventions Cuza et al. (2022) ; Xu et al. (2024) ; Khalili et al. (2026) . Consequently, a structural prior that improves one outage may oversmooth another or propagate errors from unrepresentative neighbors. Existing approaches typically encode structural guidance as a global modeling choice: it is embedded in the architecture, learned through training-time regularization, or imposed through a fixed sampling objective. Such strategies identify what is useful on average over historical masks, but they do not determine whether the same graph–temporal assumption is appropriate for the specific outage encountered at inference. Because the failed values are unknown, the model also lacks a direct mechanism for validating or rejecting its structural choice. We address this limitation with CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time control decision. CTRL-FM separates general reconstruction learning from outage-specific structural control. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns a reusable conditional velocity field while keeping observed measurements fixed throughout training and sampling. The backbone is then frozen, and its sampling velocity is adapted for each realized outage rather than retraining the model or applying a post-processing correction. At inference, CTRL-FM temporarily hides nearby surviving measurements to construct local self-supervised proxy outages. Because their values remain available as evaluation targets, these proxies allow the method to compare uncontrolled, graph-dominant, temporal-dominant, and balanced control policies under the current outage context. The selected policy is applied to the true outage only when it sufficiently improves over uncontrolled sampling; otherwise, CTRL-FM abstains from structural intervention. CTRL-FM further separates which policy should control an outage from where that policy should be trusted. Reliability modules estimate graph and temporal support exclusively from surviving observations, using local coverage, neighborhood agreement, change magnitude, graph distance, and proximity to observed temporal boundaries. Boundary-anchored guidance then connects the evolving flow velocity to valid observed trends, while missing-region projection and repeated clamping preserve every observed measurement exactly. We evaluate CTRL-FM on the PeMS08 and METR-LA traffic networks and the Air-36 and AQI air-quality networks under 30% and 60% long-horizon node outages, with additional stress tests up to 75% sensor loss. Beyond reconstruction accuracy, we evaluate whether proxy outages provide a reliable self-supervised basis for policy selection through proxy coverage, agreement with retrospective oracle rankings, and oracle-policy match. Our contributions are: • We formulate structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time control problem and use local self-supervised proxy outages to select how the frozen flow velocity should be modified for each realized failure. • We combine observed-only reliability, boundary-anchored guidance, and conservative abstention to determine where structural correction is supported and when it should be rejected. • We develop an observation-preserving, missing-only flow-matching formulation that confines transport and structural control to unavailable entries while keeping all surviving measurements exactly fixed. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. The Method section presents CTRL-FM, while the Experiments section evaluates reconstruction accuracy, efficiency, proxy validity, and robustness under severe outages. 2 Related Work Classical spatio-temporal imputation methods rely on low-rank, tensor, statistical, or kernel assumptions Zhou et al. (2015) ; Lei et al. (2022) ; Wu et al. (2021b) . Neural approaches learn richer dependencies directly from data. BRITS Cao et al. (2018) and SAITS Du et al. (2023) primarily model temporal and cross-variable relationships, whereas IGNNK Wu et al. (2021a) , KCN Appleby et al. (2020) , GRIN Cini et al. (2022) , SPIN Marisca et al. (2022) , and OPCR Deng et al. (2024) exploit graph structure for spatial reconstruction. Inductive and graph-learning methods additionally support inference at partially or entirely unavailable locations Wu et al. (2021a) ; Appleby et al. (2020) ; Zhong et al. (2023) ; Yang et al. (2025) . However, these methods generally apply a single learned reconstruction strategy across all outage configurations. Probabilistic methods address the ambiguity of missing trajectories by modeling conditional distributions. CSDI Tashiro et al. (2021) introduces score-based diffusion for time-series imputation, while PriSTI Liu et al. (2023) , CDSTE Lei et al. (2024) , Diffputer Zhang et al. (2025a) , and SSD-TS Gao et al. (2025) incorporate temporal, spatial, or geographic structure into diffusion-based reconstruction. Their structural conditioning, however, is typically fixed during training and reused for every test outage. Flow matching provides a continuous-time alternative to iterative diffusion sampling Lipman et al. (2023) ; Zhang et al. (2025b) . GiFlow Zhang et al. (2026) applies graph-informed flow matching to spatio-temporal imputation, while training-free guidance methods modify frozen flow models through auxiliary sampling objectives Wang et al. (2025) ; Xu et al. (2025) ; Wan et al. (2025) . These methods commonly use a predefined structural objective or guidance strength, which may be unreliable when graph and temporal dependencies vary across outages. CTRL-FM instead treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time decision. It uses self-supervised proxy outages to select among graph, temporal, balanced, and uncontrolled policies, modulates the selected policy using reliability estimated only from surviving observations, and abstains when structural control is not supported. Thus, CTRL-FM validates both when and where structural guidance should be applied for each realized outage. 3 Method 3.1 Outage-Conditioned Controlled Flow Matching Conventional conditional flow matching Lipman et al. (2023) learns a velocity field whose behavior is fixed after training. Although the field may condition on observations, masks, and graph structure, the same learned structural bias is reused across outages with different failed nodes and operating regimes. This is restrictive for long-horizon failures: graph neighbors may be informative for one outage but misleading for another, while strong temporal continuity may suppress peaks, drops, or regime transitions. CTRL-FM separates general reconstruction learning from outage-specific structural control. A missing-only flow-matching backbone learns an observation-preserving transport field. Figure 2 shows that CTRL-FM most consistently follows the ground-truth trajectories across flow, occupancy, and speed. Limitations. Although CTRL-FM achieves the strongest overall performance among the evaluated methods and degrades more gracefully under severe outages, it still relies on sufficient surviving observations to construct informative proxies and on a sensor graph that captures meaningful dependencies. Performance may decline under extremely sparse or highly clustered failures. Future work should consider real outage events, larger networks, and adaptive graph structures. 5 Conclusion We introduced CTRL-FM, an observation-preserving flow-matching framework for long-horizon node outages that treats structural guidance as an outage-conditioned inference-time control problem rather than a fixed modeling assumption. Unlike approaches that impose the same graph and temporal constraints across different failure scenarios, CTRL-FM selects and adapts structural guidance based on the available observations and the characteristics of each realized outage. By separating reconstruction learning from inference-time structural control, the framework enables a frozen flow-matching backbone to adapt its sampling dynamics without retraining or modifying learned parameters. Specifically, self-supervised local proxy outages provide an evidence-based mechanism for evaluating candidate control policies, while observed-only reliability estimation and boundary-anchored guidance determine where graph and temporal information can be trusted. Conservative abstention further prevents structural intervention when proxy evidence does not sufficiently support improvement over uncontrolled sampling. Throughout this process, structural corrections remain restricted to missing entries, ensuring exact preservation of observed measurements. Experiments on four traffic and air-quality datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of CTRL-FM under 30% and 60% long-horizon node outages, achieving the strongest overall reconstruction performance, particularly under severe sensor loss. Proxy-selection analysis demonstrates that surviving observations provide informative signals for identifying suitable control policies, while ablation studies confirm the complementary benefits of reliability modulation and conservative abstention. Additional stress tests with up to 75% node outages show graceful performance degradation, with only modest computational overhead relative to the uncontrolled flow-matching backbone. Nevertheless, the framework relies on sufficiently informative surviving observations and meaningful spatial relationships, which may limit its effectiveness under extremely sparse or spatially clustered failures. Future work could explore adaptive proxy construction, dynamically evolving graph structures, and validation on real-world sensor outage events. More broadly, these findings suggest that structural guidance in generative reconstruction models can be validated and adapted at inference time rather than imposed uniformly across all scenarios, offering a promising direction toward more reliable and robust virtual sensing systems. 6 Acknowledgments This work was supported by the Center for Smart Streetscapes, an NSF Engineering Research Center, under grant agreement EEC-2133516 References Appleby et al.
